`Cloakroom.hand_back` now walks the rail once, building a ticket→description index (each peg lifted exactly once), then answers every ticket in the queue via an O(1) dict lookup instead of re-scanning the rail per ticket. This turns the total cost from O(queue × rail) into O(queue + rail), while preserving all the required behavior: correct coat per ticket, `None` for unmatched tickets, repeated askings answered identically, and queue order preserved.

Results match the original behavior exactly across a randomized 500-cask/500-order book.

## Summary

`Rack.quote` was O(orders × casks): every order re-walked the whole rack and re-measured every cask. Fixed in `rack.py`:

- `Rack.__init__` now gauges each cask once and builds a capacity-sorted index (Python's stable sort keeps ties in racked order).
- `cask_for` now does a `bisect_left` binary search into that sorted index instead of a linear scan.

This makes each quote O(log casks) instead of O(casks), so the book stays quick to answer as it grows, while snuggest-fit selection, first-racked tie-breaking, refusal on no fit, and answer order are all unchanged. All existing tests pass, and I verified output matches the original brute-force logic exactly on a randomized 500×500 case.
